extracted.intended_audience: scientists (geologists and experimental physicists); readers of Nature
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptions and methodological guidance for performing and reporting a bench acoustics experiment (tuning-fork demonstration of Doppler effect) and accompanying geological-historical review; emphasizes experimental setup, controls, measurements, and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure true unison of tuning forks
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that forks 1 and 2 should really be in unison.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on sounding two forks together (they may force each other into a common oscillation). Use three forks: load one so it gives 2–3 beats per second with one of the others; determine the interval occupied by 20–30 beats with a chronograph (e.g., Casella’s registering stop-watch); compare intervals and adjust the quicker fork by adding wax until intervals match. When carefully adjusted, projection effects (e.g., launching the cork ball) are reproducible at large distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insulate and mount forks to avoid mechanical coupling
rubrics_metrics.description: Forks are supported on india-rubber tubing and thus insulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mounting on india-rubber tubing isolates forks mechanically so they do not constrain one another; this insulation is part of obtaining true independent frequencies prior to unison adjustment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use beat-counting and chronograph for frequency adjustment
rubrics_metrics.description: Adjust forks by comparing beats over many cycles and timing with a chronograph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the interval for 20–30 beats to accurately determine frequency differences; adjust by loading with wax (or by filing) until the desired beat-rate (e.g., zero beats when in unison, or two beats/sec difference for test forks) is achieved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detection method: suspended cork ball specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: A small cork ball (5 or 6"™ diameter) suspended by a silk fibre just touching a prong serves as a qualitative detector of fork motion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make the cork as nearly spherical as possible so it always just touches the fork irrespective of rotation; smooth and varnish the cork to eliminate asperities that act as buffers; suspend by one or two unspun silk fibres; position so the ball just touches a prong and project its image with a lantern onto a screen for visual observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative sensitive detector: light-plane mirror method
rubrics_metrics.description: A light plane mirror held between two stretched vertical fibres, with its edge touching the fork, can detect vibrations by reflecting a beam to a screen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This mirror method (attributed to Prof. O. N. Rood) is described as an ingenious and most delicate device, useful when greater sensitivity is required than the cork-ball projection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controlled translation (uniform motion) of vibrating body to demonstrate Doppler shift
rubrics_metrics.description: Translation of a vibrating body causes it to give a different wavelength than when stationary; uniform motion of the fork/case is required to observe the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A moving case provides the necessary translation; there is a narrow range of proper velocity (reported ~8–9 feet/sec in these experiments) at which an approaching or receding fork with a slight frequency offset will produce the effect (e.g., a fork giving 254 v/s moving toward a listener at that velocity mimics 256 v/s from a stationary source). Greatly increasing or decreasing the velocity abolishes the effect. A machine to give uniform motion is recommended for quantitative investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document and report experimental geometry and distances
rubrics_metrics.description: Specify distances, orientations and relative motions (e.g., fork positions, distance 30–60 ft, moving-case movement) so effects can be interpreted and repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experiments reported include precise actions (e.g., holding fork 2 in hand 30–60 ft away; walking toward/away while screwing fork on/off its case; placing the fork on the case while in motion). Report whether the moving fork was placed on or removed from its case, the time of stopping/starting, and the ear/eye observation points (assistant’s ear close to case while eye on screen).

rubrics_metrics.name: Frequency modification techniques (weighting or filing)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modify fork frequencies by adding wax to a prong (to slow) or filing prong ends (to speed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: fork No. 3 had one prong weighted with wax to give two beats/sec less than fork 1; fork No. 4 had prong ends filed to give two beats/sec more. Use these controlled offsets to create reproducible beat relationships for Doppler demonstrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare projectile surface to avoid energy loss at impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Varnish the cork ball to give a firm coating and remove minute asperities that buffer impacts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Varnish does not sensibly increase weight but prevents elastic projections on the cork surface from deadening impacts; this improves projection distance and reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative calculation and reporting of wave/velocity relations
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate vibration counts, wave-lengths and propagation speed when interpreting results quantitatively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use known speed of sound for temperature (example: 1,118 ft/s at 60°F) and compute wavelength A = velocity / frequency; show how a moving source with frequency n' and velocity v produces the observed received frequency, and use these relations to estimate required source velocities for observed shifts (analogy given to optical frequencies and stellar motions). Report assumed constants and calculation steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report sensitivity limits and reproducibility claims
rubrics_metrics.description: State achievable sensitivity and reproducibility for the described setup and what improvements are planned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author reports projecting cork ball at 60 ft reproducibly and believes 100 ft possible given careful adjustment; describes a planned machine for uniform translation for quantitative work; these claims should be accompanied by the detailed conditions and apparatus so others can reproduce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Geological classification must be grounded in correct stratigraphical and fossil evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Geological systems and nomenclature should be accepted only when physical sectional evidence and fossil relations are correctly understood.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical example: Murchison’s Silurian system was criticized because sectional evidence was misunderstood leading to inverted sequences; Sedgwick argued that geologists 'would [not] have accepted the Lower Silurian classification and nomenclature, had they known that the physical or sectional evidence ... had been from the first positively misunderstood.' Thus classifications should be based on correctly interpreted sections and fossil identifications (cross-regional tracing).

rubrics_metrics.name: Maps, legends and abstracts must not be altered without author inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Changes made to an author's map or its legend (or abstracts) without the author's inspection or consent compromise the work's integrity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical case: Sedgwick’s reduced map was altered (legend changed to conform with another author's nomenclature) without his knowledge; proofs of abstracts were not made available to the author. Best practice: allow authors to inspect proofs and avoid unilateral renaming or recoloring that misrepresents the author's conclusions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Subdivide lithostratigraphic units only on paleontological/stratigraphic grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide formations or groups when palaeontological evidence (distinct faunas) or clear stratigraphic relations justify subdivision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Salter’s subdivision of the Lingula flags into upper/middle/lower units based on characteristic fossils; Barrande’s Etage divisions named from characteristic trilobite genera. Explicit fossil assemblages should be used to justify subunits and correlations across regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correlate strata across regions using characteristic fossil genera
rubrics_metrics.description: Use presence/absence and identity of characteristic genera (e.g., Paradoxides, Olenus, Agnostus) to correlate horizons between different areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper uses fossil genera to tie strata in Scandinavia, Bohemia, and Britain (e.g., Paradoxides linking Menevian beds to Barrande’s Etage C). When correlating, report which diagnostic taxa are present and whether ranges are continuous or constrained.
